To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) molecular dynamics simulations are computationally more efficient if they are performed in small boxes, (ii) molecular dynamics simulations in large systems are not necessarily more efficient than simulations in small systems, and (iii) the reduced-order method is a promising approach to reduce computational costs of microscopic simulations in HMM.

the molecular simulations should be performed at elevated viscosity, that the time step should be chosen to be of the order of the inverse of the smallest frequency in the system, and that finite-size effects should be considered.

molecular dynamics simulations in hybrid multiscale schemes are best carried out using small systems, a simple thermostat, small time steps and a reduced-order technique for coupling to the macroscopy solver.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of efficient hybrid schemes and the identification of pitfalls and caveats which are relevant in the context of multiscale simulations of soft matter.
a detailed analysis of the microscopic simulations in hybrid particle–continuum schemes.

the design of efficient and robust multiscale schemes for the simulation of soft matter liquids, and the results are applicable to a wide range of applications in the field of heterogeneous multiscale methods.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the choice of a molecular simulation scheme for the coupling is highly problem dependent, and that the choice of the scheme should be based on a detailed analysis of the specific problem at hand.
the molecular dynamics simulation is not a bottleneck in heterogeneous multiscale methods, and that the molecular dynamics simulations can be run in a way which is computationally efficient.

the computational effort of molecular dynamics simulations in HMM schemes can be significantly decreased by a proper choice of the molecular simulation parameters and by using a reduced-order stress–strain relation for the coupling.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in the context of heterogeneous multiscale methods, molecular dynamics simulations can be performed efficiently, but the choice of parameters is important.
, in general, molecular dynamics simulations in hybrid schemes are feasible, but require some careful consideration of the above mentioned pitfalls.
the use of molecular simulations in heterogeneous multiscale methods is not only possible but also very efficient, as long as one is careful about the choice of parameters.
The main takeaway from our work is that
molecular dynamics simulations can serve as the basis of HMM, but that care has to be taken when choosing the simulation parameters.

molecular simulations in heterogeneous schemes can be carried out efficiently, and the computational bottleneck is not necessarily in the molecular simulations but rather in the macroscopic simulations.

molecular simulations are computationally efficient in HMM schemes if the microscopic simulations are performed carefully, which is demonstrated by the fact that we are able to simulate a microfluidic device with a channel of length 1 mm and width of 10 µm with only 10 6 particles.
